answer.summary: Zhang says an MVP that merely works may not be enough: a minimal lovable product meets the quality bar that resonates with its users. That can mean delivering fewer things exceptionally well, with the right bar depending on what users are replacing and what alternatives they have.

sections.heading: The distinction
sections.content: A minimal viable product may meet a basic usability bar; a minimal lovable product is good, polished, and feels like it truly meets users’ needs. Zhang frames minimal lovable as the new MVP, especially when users have many alternatives.

sections.heading: Set the bar for the users and context
sections.content: Lovability is relative to what users are trying to do and what they currently use. If a product replaces a painful manual workflow such as spreadsheets, it may be lovable without many extra features. Users can also have different expectations: designers may demand a higher workflow bar, while finance or IT users may value a product that is simply much better than their current process.

sections.heading: Prioritize quality over breadth
sections.content: Rather than doing a little of everything across 15 features, Zhang favors doing five things very well, with polish and a strong fit to user needs. Small touches can help: she cites keyboard shortcuts for Webflow power users and Airbnb templates that could be pre-populated with users’ existing content. In Webflow’s memberships and logic work, the team considered whether to release what was viable and let its ecosystem help supply the lovable parts when further work risked diminishing returns.

answer.summary: Zhang says an MVP should not merely clear a bare usability bar: an MLP reaches the quality level that resonates with its users, judged against their alternatives and expectations. That can mean fewer features done exceptionally well rather than many features done only adequately.

sections.heading: Core distinction
sections.content: Zhang argues that when users have many alternatives, a product that merely “barely meets a quality bar” may not be compelling. A minimal lovable product identifies and meets the quality bar for an experience users actually love; in her words, it is the new MVP.

sections.heading: The bar depends on users and alternatives
sections.content: The required polish depends on what users are replacing and what they expect. If the alternative is a poor manual workflow, such as spreadsheets, a simpler product can already be usable and lovable, so adding 15 more features may be unnecessary. Users such as designers may have a higher workflow bar than finance or IT users accustomed to cumbersome processes.

sections.heading: Depth over breadth
sections.content: She describes an MLP as doing some parts of the experience especially well rather than doing a little of everything: for example, five highly polished features that clearly meet needs instead of 15 merely viable ones. Her examples of added quality include Webflow keyboard shortcuts that delight power users and Airbnb mobile-app templates that could be pre-populated with users’ existing content.

points.explanation: Zhang contrasts doing a few things exceptionally well, with polish, against doing many things only adequately. The answer clearly captures this depth-over-breadth distinction.
The answer says the quality bar depends on users’ expectations and what they are replacing, including the different bars she describes for designers versus finance or IT users.

answer.summary: Zhang says a minimal lovable product meets the quality bar that resonates with its users—not merely a bare viability bar. That bar depends on users’ alternatives and expectations; teams can focus on fewer features and make them genuinely good rather than offer many clunky ones.

sections.heading: The distinction
sections.content: A minimal viable product may only barely meet a quality bar. Zhang argues that this can be insufficient, especially when users have many alternatives. A minimal lovable product is the smallest product experience that feels good and meets the quality bar users care about; in her words, it is the new MVP.

sections.heading: The bar depends on context
sections.content: “Lovable” is relative to what users are replacing and what they expect. If the alternative is a manual workflow such as spreadsheets, a simpler product may already be perfectly usable and lovable, so adding many more features may not be worth delaying launch. A designer may expect a higher workflow bar than someone on a finance or IT team accustomed to a cumbersome process.

sections.heading: Do fewer things well
sections.content: Rather than build a little of everything—her example contrasts 15 minimally viable areas with five done with high polish and a strong fit to users’ needs—teams can concentrate on the parts of the experience that matter most. Small touches can help: Zhang mentions Webflow keyboard shortcuts for power users and, in Airbnb’s mobile-app revamp, templates that could be pre-populated with users’ existing content.
